Circumlocution is the act of saying something in a roundabout, indirect way using more words than necessary, when the same idea could have been expressed much more simply and directly.

Think of it like taking a long, winding detour to reach a destination you could have reached in a straight line. Instead of going straight to the point, a person "goes around" it — circling the idea without landing on it cleanly.
The Core Idea, Explained Simply

Imagine someone asks you: "Is Sarah married?"

A direct answer would be: "No, she's single."

A circumlocutory answer would be: "Well, as far as her current personal situation goes, and to the best of my knowledge regarding her relationship status at this point in time, she has not, at least not yet, entered into the institution of matrimony."

Both sentences carry the exact same information. But the second one buries a simple fact under a pile of unnecessary words and phrases. That burying — that verbal going-around — is circumlocution.
What Makes It "Circumlocution" and Not Just "Being Wordy"?

Wordiness is a broad term for using too many words. Circumlocution is more specific. It refers particularly to the avoidance of directness — the idea that you are going around the point rather than simply stating it. The excess words aren't random filler; they form an indirect path that orbits the real message without stating it plainly.

So circumlocution always involves:

  • A point that could be stated directly
  • A deliberate or habitual choice to state it indirectly instead
  • More words than the idea actually requires
Why Do People Use Circumlocution?

Circumlocution isn't always a mistake or a bad habit. It has several causes, and some of them are very human and understandable.

1. To avoid saying something uncomfortable
Sometimes people don't want to say something blunt because it feels harsh, rude, or painful. Instead of saying "You're fired," a manager might say "We are going to be moving forward in a direction that no longer includes your role in the organizational structure." The uncomfortable truth is still there — it's just wrapped in layers of softer language.

2. To sound more impressive or formal
Some people use long, winding language to sound educated, authoritative, or sophisticated. A politician, for example, might say "We are committed to exploring all available avenues with respect to the potential restructuring of our budgetary allocations" — when they really just mean "We might cut spending."

3. Bureaucratic or legal habit
In formal institutions — governments, corporations, legal systems — circumlocution often becomes a deeply ingrained style. Officials learn to speak and write in vague, indirect language because it protects them from being pinned down to a specific commitment. Charles Dickens famously satirized this in his novel Bleak House, where he invented the "Circumlocution Office" — a fictional government department whose entire purpose was to avoid getting anything done by drowning everything in paperwork and indirect language.

4. Genuine uncertainty or tact
Sometimes circumlocution reflects honest caution — when someone doesn't want to make a claim they're not sure of, or when they are trying to be sensitive about a difficult topic.

5. Bad habits in writing or speaking
Sometimes people simply haven't trained themselves to be concise. They pad their sentences unconsciously, repeating ideas in different words, adding qualifiers where none are needed, and filling space without realizing it.
When Is Circumlocution Acceptable?

Circumlocution is not always bad. There are situations where indirectness serves a real purpose:

  • In diplomacy, saying something directly can cause offense or damage relationships. Diplomatic circumlocution softens messages so they can be received without triggering conflict.
  • In literature and poetry, a writer might intentionally circle an idea to create mood, suspense, or beauty. Not every sentence needs to be efficient.
  • In social situations, we often soften bad news or criticism out of kindness. "I think there might be a few areas where this could be improved a little" is kinder than "This is bad."

In these cases, circumlocution is a social and rhetorical tool — used deliberately and skillfully.
When Is Circumlocution a Problem?

Circumlocution becomes a genuine problem when:

  • It obscures the truth — either to deceive or to avoid accountability
  • It wastes the listener's or reader's time unnecessarily
  • It makes communication confusing or exhausting to follow
  • It is used to hide a lack of substance — covering up an empty idea with a flood of words

In writing, circumlocution is one of the most common signs of unclear thinking. When a writer hasn't fully worked out what they want to say, they often produce long, winding sentences that circle the idea without ever clearly stating it. Good editors and writing teachers train people to hunt for circumlocution and cut it.
How to Spot Circumlocution

Here are the telltale signs of circumlocution in speech or writing:

  • A sentence is very long, but its core message is very simple
  • The speaker or writer keeps adding qualifiers: "in a manner of speaking," "at this point in time," "with respect to," "in terms of," etc.
  • After reading or hearing a sentence, you have to work hard to figure out what was actually being said
  • You could cut more than half the words and lose nothing important
  • The person seems to be saying something, but you can't quite pin down what
Synonyms and Related Words

To round out your understanding, here are words and phrases that are closely related to circumlocution. They each carry a slightly different shade of meaning, but all orbit the same idea:

  • Periphrasis — almost identical in meaning; the use of more words than necessary to express something. (More commonly used in grammar and linguistics.)
  • Verbosity / Verbiage — the quality of using too many words in general.
  • Prolixity — excessive length and wordiness in speech or writing.
  • Roundaboutness — the informal, everyday way of describing the same quality.
  • Beating around the bush — the common idiom that captures circumlocution perfectly in everyday language.
Using the Word in Sentences

To make the word feel natural, here is how "circumlocution" (and its related forms) are used in real sentences:

  • "His circumlocution was so extreme that by the time he finished speaking, no one could remember what his original point had been."
  • "The politician's answer was pure circumlocution — five minutes of talking without saying a single concrete thing."
  • "Good writing requires the elimination of circumlocution; say what you mean, then stop."
  • "She resorted to circumlocution because she didn't want to tell him directly that he hadn't got the job."
  • "The legal document was full of circumlocutions that made it nearly impossible for an ordinary person to understand."

The adjective form is circumlocutory ("a circumlocutory response") and the adverb is circumlocutorily — though in everyday use, most people simply say "indirect" or "roundabout" instead.
The One-Line Summary

If you want to remember this word forever, hold onto this:

Circumlocution is the art of using ten words to say what one word would have said perfectly well.
